claim: Usher syndrome type I (USH1) is characterized by deafness, vestibular areflexia, and progressive retinal degeneration.
source: Usher syndrome type I (USH1) is characterized by deafness, vestibular areflexia, and progressive retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about USH1 that draws from established scientific knowledge about the syndrome.

claim: The protein-truncating p.Arg245* founder variant of PCDH15 (USH1F) has an ~2% carrier frequency amongst Ashkenazi Jews.
source: The protein-truncating p.Arg245* founder variant of PCDH15 (USH1F) has an ~2% carrier frequency amongst Ashkenazi Jews accounts for ~60% of their USH1 cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ben-Yosef et al., 2003 in the Introduction section.

claim: The p.Arg245* variant accounts for ~60% of USH1 cases in Ashkenazi Jews.
source: The protein-truncating p.Arg245* founder variant of PCDH15 (USH1F) has an ~2% carrier frequency amongst Ashkenazi Jews accounts for ~60% of their USH1 cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ben-Yosef et al., 2003 in the Introduction section.

claim: Longitudinal phenotyping in 13 USH1F individuals revealed progressive retinal degeneration, leading to severe vision loss with macular atrophy by the sixth decade.
source: Here, longitudinal phenotyping in 13 USH1F individuals revealed progressive retinal degeneration, leading to severe vision loss with macular atrophy by the sixth decade.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1 showing patient outcomes over time.

claim: Half of the affected individuals were legally blind by their mid-50s.
source: Half of the affected individuals were legally blind by their mid-50s.
evidence: This is supported by the Kaplan-Meier survival curves shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The mouse Pcdh15R250X variant is equivalent to human p.Arg245*.
source: The mouse Pcdh15R250X variant is equivalent to human p.Arg245*.
evidence: This is based on the design of the mouse model using CRISPR/Cas9 to create the equivalent mutation.

claim: Homozygous Pcdh15R250X mice have visual deficits.
source: Homozygous Pcdh15R250X mice also have visual deficits and aberrant light-dependent translocation of the phototransduction cascade proteins, arrestin, and transducin.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating reduced amplitudes in mutant mice.

claim: Homozygous Pcdh15R250X mice have aberrant light-dependent translocation of arrestin and transducin.
source: Homozygous Pcdh15R250X mice also have visual deficits and aberrant light-dependent translocation of the phototransduction cascade proteins, arrestin, and transducin.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RPE65 and CRALBP were reduced in Pcdh15R250X mice.
source: Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-specific retinoid cycle proteins, RPE65 and CRALBP, were also reduced in Pcdh15R250X mice, indicating a dual role for protocadherin-15 in photoreceptors and RPE.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3b and quantification in Figure 3c.

claim: Protocadherin-15 has a dual role in photoreceptors and RPE.
source: Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-specific retinoid cycle proteins, RPE65 and CRALBP, were also reduced in Pcdh15R250X mice, indicating a dual role for protocadherin-15 in photoreceptors and RPE.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced RPE proteins and aberrant protein translocation in photoreceptors.

claim: Exogenous 9-cis retinal improved ERG amplitudes in Pcdh15R250X mice.
source: Exogenous 9-cis retinal improved ERG amplitudes in Pcdh15R250X mice, suggesting a basis for a clinical trial of FDA-approved retinoids to preserve vision in USH1F patients.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4 demonstrating improved amplitudes after 9-cis retinal treatment.

claim: Usher syndrome is estimated to be responsible for more than 50% of deaf-blind cases.
source: Usher syndrome (USH) is estimated to be responsible for more than 50% of deaf-blind cases, 8–33% of patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and 3–6% of congenitally deaf individuals (Boughman et al., 1983; Brownstein et al., 2004; Vernon, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boughman et al., 1983; Brownstein et al., 2004; Vernon, 1969.

claim: Usher syndrome accounts for 8–33% of patients with retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Usher syndrome (USH) is estimated to be responsible for more than 50% of deaf-blind cases, 8–33% of patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and 3–6% of congenitally deaf individuals (Boughman et al., 1983; Brownstein et al., 2004; Vernon, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boughman et al., 1983; Brownstein et al., 2004; Vernon, 1969.

claim: Usher syndrome accounts for 3–6% of congenitally deaf individuals.
source: Usher syndrome (USH) is estimated to be responsible for more than 50% of deaf-blind cases, 8–33% of patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and 3–6% of congenitally deaf individuals (Boughman et al., 1983; Brownstein et al., 2004; Vernon, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boughman et al., 1983; Brownstein et al., 2004; Vernon, 1969.

claim: The prevalence of USH is estimated at 3.2–6.2 per 100,000.
source: Clinical data review studies estimated a prevalence of 3.2–6.2 per 100,000 for USH cases (Boughman and Fishman, 1983; Koenekoop et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boughman and Fishman, 1983; Koenekoop et al., 1993.

claim: A molecular diagnosis study in children with hearing loss found variants in USH-associated genes in 11%.
source: However, a molecular diagnosis study in children with hearing loss found variants in USH-associated genes in 11% and estimated a frequency of 1/6000 individuals afflicted with USH in the United States (Kimberling et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kimberling et al., 2010.

claim: The frequency of USH is estimated at 1/6000 individuals in the United States.
source: However, a molecular diagnosis study in children with hearing loss found variants in USH-associated genes in 11% and estimated a frequency of 1/6000 individuals afflicted with USH in the United States (Kimberling et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kimberling et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of vision in individuals with USH1 begins towards the end of their first decade of life due to retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Loss of vision in individuals with USH1, an autosomal recessive disorder, begins towards the end of their first decade of life due to RP, eventually leading to near total blindness.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vernon, 1969 and clinical data from the patient cohort.

claim: Night blindness is an early sign in USH1 subjects.
source: Night blindness is an early sign in USH1 subjects followed by constriction of the visual field (tunnel vision) and finally clinical blindness (Vernon, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vernon, 1969.

claim: Characteristic fundus features of USH1 include pigmentary retinopathy, narrowing of the retinal vessels, and a pale appearance of the optic disk.
source: Characteristic fundus features include pigmentary retinopathy, narrowing of the retinal vessels, and a pale appearance of the optic disk (Toms et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Toms et al., 2020.

claim: Vestibular dysfunction in USH1 manifests as a delay in development of independent ambulation.
source: Vestibular dysfunction in USH1 manifests as a delay in development of independent ambulation while hearing loss is usually severe to profound, congenital, and sensorineural (Ahmed et al., 2003b; Smith et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2003b; Smith et al., 1994.

claim: Hearing loss in USH1 is usually severe to profound, congenital, and sensorineural.
source: Vestibular dysfunction in USH1 manifests as a delay in development of independent ambulation while hearing loss is usually severe to profound, congenital, and sensorineural (Ahmed et al., 2003b; Smith et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2003b; Smith et al., 1994.

claim: Cochlear implants can restore auditory perception in USH1 patients.
source: Cochlear implants can restore auditory perception in USH1 patients (Brownstein et al., 2004; Pennings et al., 2006), but presently there is no effective treatment for vision loss due to RP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brownstein et al., 2004; Pennings et al., 2006.

claim: There is presently no effective treatment for vision loss due to retinitis pigmentosa in USH1.
source: Cochlear implants can restore auditory perception in USH1 patients (Brownstein et al., 2004; Pennings et al., 2006), but presently there is no effective treatment for vision loss due to RP.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of treatment options, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Eleven patients from nine families were homozygous for the p.Arg245* variant.
source: Eleven patients from nine families were homozygous for the p.Arg245*, leading to truncation of the encoded protein, protocadherin-15.
evidence: This is supported by the patient data presented in Table 1.

claim: Two patients had compound heterozygous genotypes that included one p.Arg245* allele.
source: Two additional patients had compound heterozygous genotypes that included one p.Arg245* allele.
evidence: This is supported by the patient data presented in Table 1.

claim: Protocadherin-15 is a member of a large cadherin superfamily of calcium-dependent cell–cell adhesion molecules.
source: Protocadherin-15 is a member of a large cadherin superfamily of calcium-dependent cell–cell adhesion molecules (Ahmed et al., 2001; van Roy, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2001; van Roy, 2014.

claim: Within the vertebrate inner ear, protocadherin-15 is required for the structural maintenance and the mechanotransduction function of the sensory hair cells.
source: Within the vertebrate inner ear, protocadherin-15 is required for the structural maintenance and the mechanotransduction function of the sensory hair cells (Ahmed et al., 2006; Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2006; Kazmierczak et al., 2007.

claim: In the retina, protocadherin-15 is localized to the outer limiting membrane of photoreceptors and in Müller glia.
source: In the retina, protocadherin-15 is localized to the outer limiting membrane of photoreceptors (PRs) and in Müller glia (Reiners et al., 2005b; van Wijk et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reiners et al., 2005b; van Wijk et al., 2006.

claim: A reduction of electroretinogram a- and b-waves amplitudes (~40%) at 5 weeks of age was previously reported in at least two Pcdh15 alleles in mice (Pcdh15av-5J and Pcdh15av-jfb).
source: We previously reported a reduction of electroretinogram (ERG) a- and b-waves amplitudes (~40%) at 5 weeks of age in at least two Pcdh15 alleles in mice (Pcdh15av-5J and Pcdh15av-jfb) (Haywood-Watson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haywood-Watson et al., 2006.

claim: The first reported symptom in USH1F patients was difficulty with vision at night.
source: Subsequent to congenital profound deafness, the first reported symptom was difficulty with vision at night.
evidence: This is supported by the clinical data from the patient cohort.

claim: ERG recordings were at noise-level for both scotopic and photopic responses in USH1F patients, suggesting dysfunctional photoreceptors.
source: Electroretinography (ERG) recordings were at noise-level for both scotopic and photopic responses, suggesting dysfunctional PRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In young USH1F patients with early stages of retinal degeneration, findings included mottling of the retinal pigment epithelium with early pigment redistribution, and mild to moderate vascular attenuation with typically preserved macular reflexes.
source: In young patients with early stages of the retinal degeneration, findings included mottling of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) with early pigment redistribution, and mild to moderate vascular attenuation with typically preserved macular reflexes (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by fundus images shown in Figure 1a.

claim: As retinitis pigmentosa progressed in USH1F patients, more extensive pigment abnormalities were observed with deposition of bone spicules, severe attenuation of the retinal vasculature, macular atrophic changes, and waxy pallor of the optic nerve head.
source: As RP progressed, more extensive pigment abnormalities were observed with deposition of bone spicules, severe attenuation of the retinal vasculature, macular atrophic changes, and waxy pallor of the optic nerve head (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by fundus images shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Cataracts were common in USH1F patients, especially posterior subcapsular opacities.
source: Cataracts were common, especially posterior subcapsular opacities.
evidence: This is supported by the clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: Early loss of the ability to detect the smaller and dimmer target (I1e) was observed in all but one USH1F patient.
source: Kinetic visual field testing (Table 1) showed early loss of the ability to detect the smaller and dimmer target (I1e) in all but one patient (LMG268 #1722 at age 37 years).
evidence: This is supported by visual field data presented in Table 1.

claim: Protocadherin-15 could not be detected in retinal tissue from Pcdh15R250X/R250X mutant mice using immunostaining.
source: Indeed, with immunostaining, we could not detect protocadherin-15 expression in retinal tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-b) or cochlear tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c) from Pcdh15R250X/R250X mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No auditory-evoked brainstem responses were detected in mutant Pcdh15R250X mice at P16, indicating profound deafness.
source: Consistent with previously published Pcdh15 mouse models (Alagramam et al., 2011; Garwin et al., 2000; Senften et al., 2006), we detected no auditory-evoked brainstem responses (ABRs) in mutant Pcdh15R250X mice at P16, the earliest postnatal day that ABRs can be reliably detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), indicating that they were profoundly deaf.
evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and citations to previous studies.

claim: Pcdh15R250X mutant mice displayed abnormal motor vestibular behaviors such as circling, hyperactivity, and head bobbing.
source: Furthermore, Pcdh15R250X mutant mice displayed abnormal motor vestibular behaviors such as circling, hyperactivity, and head bobbing.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b, c.

claim: Pcdh15R250X mutant cochlear and vestibular hair cells had no functional mechanotransduction.
source: Finally the Pcdh15R250X mutant cochlear and vestibular hair cells also had no functional mechanotransduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d), accounting for deafness, and at P60 also showed degeneration of hair cells in the organ of Corti (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by FM1-43 uptake data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claim: At P60, Pcdh15R250X mutant mice showed degeneration of hair cells in the organ of Corti.
source: Finally the Pcdh15R250X mutant cochlear and vestibular hair cells also had no functional mechanotransduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d), accounting for deafness, and at P60 also showed degeneration of hair cells in the organ of Corti (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dark-adapted ERG waves showed normal wave architecture albeit with reduced amplitudes in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice.
source: Dark-adapted (scotopic) ERG waves, which are preferentially driven by rod PRs at low light intensity and by rod and cone PRs at high light intensity, showed normal wave architecture albeit with reduced amplitudes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is supported by ERG waveform data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a.

claim: Significant reduction in amplitudes of the a-wave and b-wave were observed in 1-month-old Pcdh15R250X mutant mice compared to littermate control mice.
source: Quantification showed significant reduction in amplitudes of the a-wave derived primarily from the PR layer and the b-wave derived from Müller glia and bipolar neurons in 1-month-old Pcdh15R250X mutant mice as compared to littermate control mice (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by ERG quantification data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Photopic ERG amplitudes were reduced in 1-month-old Pcdh15R250X mutant mice.
source: Similarly, photopic ERG amplitudes, primarily representing cone-mediated function, were also reduced in 1-month-old Pcdh15R250X mutant mice (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by ERG quantification data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The b- to a-wave ratio was similar across genotypes, indicating that deficits were manifested mainly at the photoreceptor level.
source: The b- to a-wave ratio (b/a) was similar across genotypes indicating that deficits were manifested mainly at the PR level (Figure 2—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is supported by b/a ratio data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4b and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Pcdh15R250X mutant mice consistently had lower scotopic and photopic ERG amplitudes compared to controls at 2–3, 6–7, and 12–14 months of age.
source: Pcdh15R250X mutant mice consistently had lower scotopic and photopic ERG amplitudes compared to controls (Figure 2c–h), indicating that the functional deficits observed at 1 month were not due to delayed development.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 2c–h.

claim: Equivalent recovery of a-wave was observed irrespective of genotype after bleaching of more than 90% of rhodopsin.
source: We observed equivalent recovery of a-wave irrespective of genotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c), but we did observe that initial single flash a-wave amplitude was lower in mutant mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d), which suggests functional alterations in phototransduction such as are indicated by aberrant light-dependent translocation of arrestin and transducin (see details below).
evidence: This is supported by dark adaptation recovery data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4c.

claim: Initial single flash a-wave amplitude was lower in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice.
source: We observed equivalent recovery of a-wave irrespective of genotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c), but we did observe that initial single flash a-wave amplitude was lower in mutant mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d), which suggests functional alterations in phototransduction such as are indicated by aberrant light-dependent translocation of arrestin and transducin (see details below).
evidence: This is supported by pre-bleach a-wave data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4d.

claim: OCT showed no gross structural abnormality in homozygous Pcdh15R250X mutants in young (1–2 months) and old (12–14 months) mice.
source: To correlate functional deficits with the structural integrity of the retina, we performed non-invasive in vivo retinal imaging using optical coherence tomography (OCT) in young (1–2 months) and old (12–14 months) mice, which showed no gross structural abnormality in homozygous Pcdh15R250X mutants (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by OCT images shown in Figure 2i.

claim: A small but significant decrease in the outer nuclear layer thickness was observed in 12–14 months old Pcdh15R250X mutant mice.
source: However, we did note a small but significant decrease in the outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in 12–14 months old mutant mice (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is supported by ONL thickness quantification shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Protocadherin-15 is expressed in the RPE.
source: Using immunohistochemistry, here we show that protocadherin-15 is also expressed in the RPE (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant mislocalization of both arrestin and transducin to the photoreceptor inner and outer segments was found in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice under light-adapted conditions.
source: We found significant mislocalization of both arrestin and transducin to the PR IS and OS in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice under light-adapted conditions, whereas transducin was correctly localized only to the IS and arrestin only to the OS in control mouse retinae (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In dark-adapted conditions, arrestin was correctly localized to the inner segment and transducin to the outer segment in both mutant and control mice.
source: In dark-adapted conditions, arrestin was correctly localized to the IS and transducin to the OS in both mutant and control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, c-d).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, c-d.

claim: Opsin was correctly localized only in the outer segment under both dark- and light-adapted conditions.
source: Finally, opsin was correctly localized only in the OS under both dark- and light-adapted conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, e), indicating that protocadherin-15 is essential for rapid shuttling of proteins from IS to OS and vice-versa in response to adaptation to light.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, e.

claim: Protocadherin-15 is essential for rapid shuttling of proteins from inner segment to outer segment and vice-versa in response to adaptation to light.
source: Finally, opsin was correctly localized only in the OS under both dark- and light-adapted conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, e), indicating that protocadherin-15 is essential for rapid shuttling of proteins from IS to OS and vice-versa in response to adaptation to light.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that arrestin and transducin mislocalize in mutants but opsin does not.

claim: Immunoblotting revealed significantly reduced quantities of RPE65 and CRALBP, but not IRBP in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice.
source: Intriguingly, immunoblotting revealed significantly reduced quantities of RPE65 and CRALBP, but not IRBP in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3b and quantification in Figure 3c.

claim: Reduced levels of retinoids, particularly 11-cis-retinaloxime, were found in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice compared to controls after overnight dark adaptation.
source: We also quantified the absolute retinoid levels within the eyes after overnight dark adaptation, and as compared to controls found reduced levels of retinoids, particularly 11-cis-retinaloxime, in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by retinoid quantification data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy showed no gross structural deficits in the RPE of Pcdh15R250X mutant mice.
source: Transmission electron microscopy showed no gross structural deficits in the RPE (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by TEM images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A single treatment of Pcdh15R250X mutant mice with 9-cis retinal was sufficient to increase their ERG amplitudes to levels comparable to those in vehicle-injected wild-type controls.
source: Remarkably, a single treatment of Pcdh15R250X mutant mice with 9-cis retinal was sufficient to increase their ERG amplitudes to levels comparable to those in vehicle-injected wild-type (WT) controls (Figure 4a–b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4a–b.

claim: 9-cis retinal treatment improved cone function in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice to levels of vehicle-injected control mice.
source: Similarly, we also observed an improvement in cone function to levels of the vehicle-injected control mice (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by photopic ERG data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: By 2 weeks after 9-cis retinal treatment, the impact of exogenous retinoid treatment on ERG improvements was reduced.
source: We found that by 2 weeks after 9-cis retinal treatment, the impact of exogenous retinoid treatment on ERG improvements was reduced (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Exogenous 9-cis retinal treatment did not improve translocation of arrestin and transducin in Pcdh15R250X mutant mice.
source: We found mislocalization of arrestin and transducin in mutant mice injected with 9-cis retinal as well (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The spectrum and longitudinal ophthalmic phenotypes of USH1F patients homozygous for the p.Arg245* variant consisted of a rod-cone dystrophy and are relatively uniform across this cohort of patients.
source: The spectrum and longitudinal ophthalmic phenotypes of USH1F patients homozygous for the p.Arg245* variant (or compound heterozygotes) consisted of a rod-cone dystrophy and are relatively uniform across this cohort of patients.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the clinical data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Pcdh15R250X mutant mice have a retinal dysfunction as early as 1 month after birth.
source: Pcdh15R250X mutant mice have a retinal dysfunction as early as 1 month after birth.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: In aged Pcdh15R250X mutant mice, marginal loss of outer nuclear layer thickness is observed.
source: We do not observe gross retinal damage, however, in aged mutant mice we do observe marginal loss of ONL thickness.
evidence: This is supported by OCT quantification data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Reduced levels of RPE65 were reported in Myo7a knockout mice.
source: Reduced levels of RPE65 were reported in Myo7a knockout mice (Lopes et al., 2011), a binding partner of protocadherin-15.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lopes et al., 2011.

claim: CRALBP facilitates the transport of 11-cis retinal between the RPE and the photoreceptor outer segment.
source: Further, CRALBP facilitates the transport of 11-cis retinal between the RPE and the PR OS (Saari et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saari et al., 2001.

claim: The discordance between retinal pathologies in humans and mice may be attributable to the structural differences in their photoreceptors, particularly the presence of calyceal process in humans, monkeys, and frogs, but not in rodents.
source: The discordance between retinal pathologies in humans and mice may be further attributable to the structural differences in their PRs, particularly the presence of calyceal process in humans, monkeys, and frogs, but not in rodents (Sahly et al., 2012), light exposure (Lopes et al., 2011), or environmental factors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to Sahly et al., 2012 and Lopes et al., 2011.

claim: The role of Usher proteins in the calyceal processes is supported by recent observations of photoreceptor degeneration in Ush1 frog models that have calyceal processes.
source: The role of Usher proteins in the calyceal processes is supported by recent observations of PR degeneration in Ush1 frog models that have calyceal processes (Schietroma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schietroma et al., 2017.

claim: A recent study showed degeneration of cone photoreceptors in Ush1c and Ush1g knockout mice on an albino background.
source: However, a recent study showed degeneration of cone PRs in Ush1c and Ush1g knockout mice on an albino background (Trouillet et al., 2018), which suggests that pigmentation might be providing protection to mice against the ambient light condition in their housing facilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Trouillet et al., 2018.

claim: Significant vision and photoreceptors are preserved in USH1F patients until the third decade of life.
source: Our longitudinal USH1F patient ocular data show that significant vision and PRs are preserved until the third decade of life, providing a long window of opportunity.
evidence: This is based on the clinical data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: 9-cis retinyl acetate has an excellent safety profile.
source: Our results with an 11-cis retinal analog, 9-cis retinal, raise the possibility that longer-lasting analogs such as 9-cis retinyl acetate, which has an excellent safety profile (Koenekoop et al., 2014; Scholl et al., 2015) or a synthetic version of 11-cis β-carotene, whose capsule formulation is already approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (Rotenstreich et al., 2013), could preserve vision in USH1F patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koenekoop et al., 2014; Scholl et al., 2015.

claim: A synthetic version of 11-cis β-carotene capsule formulation is already approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration.
source: Our results with an 11-cis retinal analog, 9-cis retinal, raise the possibility that longer-lasting analogs such as 9-cis retinyl acetate, which has an excellent safety profile (Koenekoop et al., 2014; Scholl et al., 2015) or a synthetic version of 11-cis β-carotene, whose capsule formulation is already approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (Rotenstreich et al., 2013), could preserve vision in USH1F patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rotenstreich et al., 2013.

claim: In mouse models lacking key visual cycle enzyme RPE65 or with the p.Pro23His variant of opsin causing retinitis pigmentosa, administration of retinoids has been shown to preserve photoreceptor morphology or proper folding of opsin to a greater extent.
source: Furthermore, in mouse models lacking key visual cycle enzyme RPE65 or with one of the most common variants of opsin causing RP (p.Pro23His), administration of retinoids has been shown to preserve PR morphology or proper folding of opsin to a greater extent (Maeda et al., 2009; Noorwez et al., 2004), and thus might also extend the life of functional PRs in USH1 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maeda et al., 2009; Noorwez et al., 2004.
